div.div:
Chapter I
After that by help ot God we hauen iended the furste partie ot this
firste Book in the whiche it is itreted ot mannis owne gouernaunce,
schewynge wherinne kynges and princes schullen sette here felicite.
For it is not semelich for hem to sette here ende in riches nother in cyuil
myght and strengthe, nother in no suche thinges, but he schal vse al suche
thinges, as it is proued totore atte folle, as instrumentis and inuen
[c]iones for to come te felicitee. thei schullen sette here felicite in dede
ot prudencia, as that dede cometh ot charite. For thanne kynges hauen
felicite accordyng to here astate, whanne by excityng of [d]eleccioun of
God, they rulen hem that bien vnder hem holilyche and rightefulliche by
prudencia ot regnynge and by lawe ot resoun. thanne the felicite of
kynges schal de principalliche iset in God. And by knowyng and loue
of hym he schal ordeyne here studie and here lit therto, that thei mowe
knowe and loue God and rule the poeple that is under ham as verrey
Goddes seruauntes by ordre of resoun.
thanne, for this is treted, and it is schewed where inne kynges schal
sette here ende and felicite by the ordre that is isette, now it is le schew
yng in what verues kynges schal be excellent and vertuous by certeyn
heyghtyng and perfeccioun of the soule. therfore it nedeth firste to
schewe whiche bien the vertual poten|cie and myghtes ot the soule and in
whiche myghtes the vertues bien igrounded and ipight. And thanne it schal
be ischewed how the vertues bien distingued. therafter we schal declare
how many suche vertues ther bien and whiche therot is principale, and
whiche is secundary, and thanne we schal trete singulerlich of eueriche
ot these vertues and how it semeth kynges and princes to haue suche
vertues.
the vertual myghtes ot the soule mowe be destyngued in these wise:
For som bien kynde and natural, and some cognitif and sensitif, and
some appetitif, and some intellectual. In natural myghtes ot the soule we
communeth with herbes and treen, as in vertual myght ot norsching, of
wexinge, and of gendrynge, and in suche as corden to herbes and treen.
the myghtes of sensitif knowing and felyng be the sight, tast, and touche
and the other wittes, and therinne we accordeth wip other bestes. the appeti
tif is destyngued, for oon appetit is in man and not in other bestes as the
appetit that foloweth the intellectual inwit. And another maner appetit
is in man and in beste, as the appetite that folweth the felyng, and suche
appetite may be cleped sensualitas. And the appetit that folweth the
intellectual inwit is icleped voluntas, the wille. And in that manere of
speche other bestes hauen the appetite that hatte sensualitas and appetitus
sensitiuus, and haueth not the appetite that hatte voluntas, the intellectual
wille
thanne the vertues ot the whiche we thinketh to speke bien goode
habites, that is dwellyng places, bien in the natural vertual
myghtes, other in the vertual myghtes and wittes ot felyng, other in the
appetite sensitif ot felyng, other in | the appetite intellectual, other in the
intellecte and inwyt, other in al thes, other in some therof. And a mowe
not be in natural vertual mighttes and that is declared in thre wise. [Firste,]
for we beth nought preysed nother iblamed for naturel and kynde vertue,
for no man is acounted a good man for he hath good degestioun and
wexinge. the seconde, suche vertues beth nought in the naturel vertual
myghtes, for suche vertues stonden by resoun as it may be preued, ii
Ethicorum, and natural myghtes bien not obedient to resoun in that thei
bien soche. For thei a man make resouns whether he wil other no, proper
liche for to speke the natural potencial vertues varieth not in here kynde
worchynge but wercheth alwey with al here myght. the thridde, habites
and vertues bien not in natural uertual myghtes, for suche habites and
vertues inclineth potencial vertues to do wel other euel, as a vicious
habite inclyneth to do euel, and as a vertuous habite inclineth to do
wel. thanne for kynde is inclyned and determined to oon, and potencial
vertues bien fol inclyned by kynde to worche by here owne kynde, and
so therby we beth nother vertuous ne vicious as we speketh heere of
vertueus and of vices; and so therinne may not be suche vertues.
And by the same thre resouns by the whiche it is preued that vertuees
bien not in the natural potencial vertues, it may be preued that thei bien
not in the knowyng ot the fif wittes. For as we ben nought ipreysed nother
iblamed for natural potencial vertues, so we ben not ipreysed nother
iblamed for the fife wittes; for as no man is preysed for a gode man for
he hath a gode digestion and wexyng, so main is [noght], presed for
scharp sight and gode hiryng, but if it falleth by hap other yf a man is ble|r
eyghed and his sight apeired for greet etyng and drynkyng, other ghif he
hath euel digestioun or feblenesse of stomachus [for etyng, aliter] he
schold be blamed [for ouer mych drinkyng, aliter] and nought for he
hath yuel dygestioun, nother for feble sight [†] - for scharp sight and
good digestioun [is not] in oure power propurliche for to speke -but
he schulde be blamed fore he hath itake to muche ot mete and of
drynke, for it was in his powere to ete and drynke mesurableliche.
the secunde, moral vertue is not in the potencial vertue ot the fyue
wyttes, for as the kynde potencial vertues beth noght obedient to reson,
for by reule ot resoun no man hath more digestioun other lasse, nother
more growyng other lasse: so the fif wittes bien not obedient to resoun,
for it is not in manis power to se other heitlerlich other dymlich; and 3if
moral vertue folweth resoun, thanne vertue is not in fife wittes,
the thridde, moral vertue is not in the fif wittes; for as the natural poten
cial vertues beth fol set to here worchyng by here owne kynde, so bien
the wittes also. For as the fuyre heteth with al his myght, for it worcheth by
his owne kynde and is therfore nother preysed nother iblamed, nother
therinne is moral vertue: so for the potencial vertue ot digestioun maketh
as gret digestioun as he may, and the eyge seeth as moche as he may.
therinne may no moral vertue be iset. For by natural vertue, potencial
vertue is iset awork atte folle by here owen kynde and nedeth therfore
no moral vertue. And so moral vertue is not in natural potencial vertue
nother in potencial vertues ot the fife wittes; and other potencial vertues
ben there nought bute the intellectualle -vertu, that is the vnderstondyng
and the appetite sensytyue and intellectiue. thanne in soche potencial
vertues mot be moral vertues.

Chapter II
For it is schewed that moral vertues ben nought in naturel potencial
vertues ot felyng, now it is to schewyng nou vertues bien distyngwed
and hon thei bien in the intellectual inwit and in the appetit. thanne il
is to distynguyng of vertues and of suche potencial vertues. For som
vertues ben intellectual, and som moral, and somme mene bytwene
intellectual and moral.
the intellectual vertues bien in the invit that hatte intellectus specula
tiuus, that is the schewing ot the inwit, and soche vertues bien speculatif
sciens, as natural philosophi, gemetrie, and methaphisik, and other
suche. And pure moral vertues bien in the appetite sensitif other intet
lectif. And soche vertues bien iusticia, temporancia, fortitudo, mansu
etudo and other soche, ot the nhiche ue schal trete syngulerlich. the
mene vertues bytwene intellectual and moral beth in the inwyt, that hatte
intellectus practicus, as prudencia and othere vertues pat longeth therto.
the comentor super libris Ethicorum seith that prudencia is acounted a
mene vertue bytwene moral vertues and intellectual vertues and may
natheles De accounted with [mor]al vertues. But prudencia is not but in
goode men as morel vertues beth not bote in gode men. Schrewed men,
theigh thei mowe be kunnynge, falce and gylefole, thei more not be
prudentes, as it schal be declared in the place therof. therfore, [vi] Eth
icorum, it is iseid that it is inpossible te be prudens and not good
thanne we leueth the vertues intellectual and sciens speculatif and
schal trete ot prudencia and ot moral vertues. For as we hauen ofte
seyd, we taken this werk not for to be kunnynge] bote for to be good,
for goodnesse may not be in vs withoute prudencia and moral vertues.
thes vertues may be in the inwit, that hatte intellectus, that is to say vnder
stondyng, and in the appetite also. And it is seid that a vertue is som
what after resoun. thanne the vertue moot be in the resonable vertue and
potencial myght. And the philosofer setteth double resonable, oon by his
owne essencia, and an other by that he is partener ot resoun. the vnder
stondyng and the inwit that hatte intellectus is resonable by his owne
essencia and by itself. And the appetit is resonable by that he is partiner
ot resoun. For theigh the appetit is not intellectus and the silf resoun, 3it he
is aconted partiner ot resoun, for he may be obedient to resoun. the
natural potencial vertues and the fif wittes ot felyng ben not resonable
of hemself, nor thei bien not the silue resoun resoun -and- [thei bien not
parteners ot resoun nor sogette to resoun] in so moche as thei bien
potencial vertues. thanne in the fif wittes and in the natural potencial
vertues bien not moral vertues, as it is iseide tofore honde; but thei bien
oonlich in the inwit and vnderstondyng, that hatte intellectus, and in the
appetite.
And in vs is double knowyng, intellectif and sensitif. For as kynde
appetite folweth kyndelich the forme that a hath by kynde, so the appetit
ot knowyng folweth the forme that apprehendeth and conceyueth by
knowyng. For as heuy thinges, for thei hauen the fourme of heuynesse,
thei hauen also a certeyne kynde inclynacioun and kynde appetit to
desire to be bynethe and lowe, so thei that hauen knowyng, in that [theil
hauen in hemself the fourme that is conceyued, thei hauen also som
inclinacioun and some appetit as that fourme moueth.
therfore as we hauen double knowyng,] sencitif and intellectif, so we
hauen doble appetit; sencitif that folweth the fourme that is conceyued by
the wit of felyng, and intellectif that is the forme that is conceyued by the
vnderstondyng, that hatte intellectus. And the appetit sencitif is double.
For bestes bien aboue soules thynges and kynde geueth double
potencial vertue to elementis and to soules thynges, oon by the whiche
thei desiren here owne reste and another by the whiche thei withstonden
thynges that letteth and bien contrary, moche more kynde igeueth to
bestes double potencial vertue, for thei bien more parfit thanne soules
thynges. We seeth that fuyre is hoot and light by kynde, and by liztnesse
desireth his owne place and quyete acordyng therto, and worcheth by
hete and withstondeth thynges that bien contrarie therto. thanne for fuyre
schulde not be ilet by contrarie thyngys to reste by liztnesse in his owne
place, kynde Seueth therto potencial vertue to hete that it may therby
worche and withstonde thinges that ben contrarie and corumpeth fyre,
than 3if kynde geueth to fyre and to soules thynges double potencial
vertue, oon by the whiche he geteth here owne quiete and reste, and
another by the whiche he worcheth and withstondeth lettes and contrarie
thynges, moche more kynde igeueth to bestes suche potencial vertues.
thanne kynde geueth to hem double appetit, sencitif appetite ot felyng,
oon by the whiche a purseweth and cometh to here owne quiete and
likynge, and this potencial vertue concupiscibilis he higte, that is coueit
isnesse; and another by the whiche he withstondeth and resfeth contrarie
and lettes, and that hatte irascibilis, as it were potencial wreth. So that the
concupiscible is as it were in stede ot lightnesse and heuynesse in list
thynges and heuy. the irascibilis is as it were in stede ot cold and ot hete
in colde] thynges and hote. For as heuye thynges by heuynesse forsaketh
the ouer place as not accordynge and cometh to the nether place as
conuenient and accordyng, and withstondeth by cold thynges that bien
contrarie and letteth and saueth hemself that they bien not corrupt in here
kynde, nother ilet ot here owne place and quiete; so by the concupis
cibilis, bestes voyden and forsaken yuel thynges and displesynge, and
folweth and taketh goode thynges and likynge. And by irascibilis a reseth
and putteth ot and wibstandeth the contrarie that myght hem lette ot suche
likynge other ot pllesanlce. By the concupiscibilis he gooth and cometh
and taketh mete as thyng that is conuenient and accordyng and likynge.
And by the irascibilis a reseth and withstondeth other that letteth hem ot
here mete.
therfore it is wel seid that the concupiscibilis taketh hede to good and
to iuel [for thei bien soche, and the irascibilis taketh hede to good and to
iuell in so moche as thei bien hard to voide othere to come to. For good
is desired for it is good, and yuel is schoned and forsake -for it is euyl
the concupiscibilis is inclined and desireth reste and thyng that is good
and likynge, and schoneth and forsaketh euel thynges and vnlikyng, and
hath for obiecte sensible goode and euel for thei bien soche (that is to
menyng al that is desired or schoned and forsake is good other euel
sensible in that that thei bien sensible). By the irascible we reseth and
withstondeth in that wyse thynges that greueth vs and letteth. And the iras
cibiles, that is wretheful doyng, longeth to good and yuel, not onlich for
they bien suche, bote for thei bien gete or kept other withstonde with
[hlafrd] diffecultee. For hard difficultee letteth vs principalliche to gete
good and voyde yuel and harme. thanne kynde rulede vnparfitliche sif
he gaf to bestes the concupiscibel to desire good and to schone and for
sake yuel, but 3if he jaf to hem also the irascibel by the whiche a reseth
and defendeth and withstondeth greues and lettes that letteth hem ot de
concupiscible in manere that is accordyng to hem, the irascibel is igeue
lectacion and likyng. thanne for bestes scholde haue ful lykynge by the
to hem by the whiche a reseth and withstondeth thynges that greueth and
letteth hem ot delectacioun and likyng. thanne the appetite sencitif of
felyng is double, irascible and concupiscible.
And the appetit intellectif that is icleped voluntas, the wille, abideth
and is on and nought deuyded. For the inwit that hatte intellectus con
ceiueth his obiecte more generallich than the wit of felyng that hinte sensus.
the appetit intellectif that folweth the inwit that histe intellectus is more
generalliche inclined to goode thynges than is the appetite that folweth the
wit ot felyng. For the more generallich a thing is take and conceyued,
to mo thynges the same thyng stryccheth. theis the appetit sencitif by the
whiche we beth inclyned and desireth sencible thynges that bien likyng
be other than the appetit sencitif by the whiche we reseth and withstondeth
greues and lettes, natheles the appetite intellectif is al oon and streccheth
to al good that is intelligible and likynge. thanne al by oon appetite in
tellectif we desiren intelligible thynges and likynge and auentreth on
thynges ot difficultee, and that appetite is not diuers as the appetite
sencitif is diuers, by the whiche we desireth sencible thynges and likynge
and wibstondeth greues and lettes.
And so 3if eueriche vertue moral is in the inwit that hatte intellectus,
other in the appetite, and som appetite is intellectif, other the wille, and
som is sencitif, and this is double, irascible and concupiscible, thanne
eueriche vertue moral mot bee] in the inwit that is intellectus, other in the
wil, other in the irascible, other in the concupiscible. ! thanne for to speke
largeliche of moral vertue, as redinesse, hatte prudencia, is acounted
vertue moral, we may saye that by these foure potencial vertues ot the
soule in the whiche beth moral vertues, foure vertues bien itake that bien
icleped cardinal vertues: that bien prudencia, iusticia, fortitudo and tem
porancia-redinesse, ristwisnesse, stalwordnesse and temporance. For
prudencia is in the intellecte, iusticia in the wille, fortitudo in the irascible
and temporancia in the concupiscible.

Chapter XIV
For it is not inow to wite and to knowe whaat manere thyng is wedloc
and how a man scholde haue hymself in wyuynge but he knowe also
how he schulde bere hymself to his wif he is iwedded, therfore to the
forseide chapitres resonabeliche this processe is annexed that we may
knowe how rewlyng ot wedloc by the whiche wyues ben irewled is
distyngwed fro othere manere rewlyng. And by twey weyes we may
declare that wifes and children ben irewled by diuers manere ofreulyng
the firste wey is itake by the manere ot reulynge, and the seconde, by
worchyng and doyng
the firste is declared in this wise. For philosofres menen that the manere
reulyng of the world is ikept and isaued in oon man, therfore among
hem man is icleped the lasse world. For as al the worlde is rewled by
oon prince and by oon God that is vnderstondyng, intellecte seuered
and pured and not bodiliche, so fal! that! is in a man, sif he scholde be
rewled thewliche, lis rewled] by intellecte (vnderstondyng) and resoun;
so that the manere ot rewelyng of the world is ikepte and isaued in eche
man, so that Plato sauede al the ordere ot heuenes in eche resonable
soule. banne 3if the rewelyng of the world is likned to the rewelyng that
scholde be in o [man, and a cyte is a partie ot the worlde, thanne the
rewelyng ot an hool cytee scholde be more ikepte and isaued in oon
hous. For sif an hous is more than oon synguler man and a cyte lasse
than the world, 3if the liknesse ot the hool world is ikepte and isaued in
oon man, moche more the liknesse ot the rewlyng ot a cyte is ikept and
isaued in oon hous. therfore, primo Poleticorum, the philosofer likneth
the rewlyng ot oon hous to the reulyng ot a cyte. And as it longeth to this
doynge, a cyte may be reuled by double manere rewlyng: by politik
rewlyng and by real rewlyng.
And he is lord by real lordschipe that is lord and rewleth by avise
ment and by lawes that he maketh and geueth and not by lawes that
citeseyns maketh. And whan a prince in a cyte is prince and lord and
maketh lawys and rewleth therby that rewlyng hath the name ot prince
other kyng and is icleped real rewlyng.
But whan nother prince ne kyng maketh the lawe but the citeseyns,
thanne rewlyng by that lawe hath not the name ot kyng nother ot prince
nother is icleped real rewlyng but it hath the name ot policye, the comynte
and of citeseyns, and is icleped politik rewelyng other cyuyle rewelyng.
And [in] Poleticlis], to thes twey manere ot rewlyng in a cyte the phi
losofer likneth twey manere reulynges ot on hous by the whiche the
fader] rewleth the child and the housebonde the wif. For the rewlyng
paternale by the whiche the fader reuleth the child is ilikned to real
rewelyng, and the rewelyng coniugale by the whiche the housebonde
scholde rewle the wif as it is ilikned to politisk] rewelyng. Folr] the house
bond schulde be aboue the wif and rewle here by politik rewelyng, for
he schuld rewle here certeyn as by lawe ot wedlok and matrimoyne
and by condiciouns and couenantes. But the fader schoulde rewle the
child by auysement and as hym liketh and by real rewlyng, for be
tweyne the fader and the childe is no couenant imaad how he scholde
be rewled. But the fader gouerneth and rewleth his child as hym liketh
and as hym semeth that it is best and most spedfol for the child as a kyng
scholde rewle his men frelich as hym semeth it is best and most spedful
for the men. Wherfore suche rewlyng is icleped real rewlyng. But alwey
bytwene housebonde and wif is som forward and couenant and som
wordes ispoke how the housebond scholde bere hym to his wif. And
therfore suche rewlyng is icleped politik rewelyng, for it is ilikned to that
rewlyng by the whiche citeseyns clepen here lord and schewen to hym
charters and dedes and couenantes that he scholde holde in his rewlyng.
thanne by the manere ot rewlyng it is declared how the oon is politik
and the other real and how the rewlyng paternale, faderlich, by the
whiche the fader rewleth the child and the rewlyng coniugale by the
which the housebond reuleth the wif ben diuerce. (For we seen that real
rewelyng is! (ful and hole and kynde rewelyng, and politik rewelyng
is! parcial rewelyng and by eleccioun. For he that reweleth realliche hap
ful and hole [rewelyng] and fre, and he that rewleth pollitiklich hath not
ful and hool rewelyng nother symple withoute condicioun but bi
certeyn condiciouns and couenantes. Also thei eche ristful rewlyng be
kynde rewlyng, ghut politic rewlyng be it neuere so riztfol it is not so
kynde rewelyng as ryal reulyng, for that rewlyng cometh in som wise by
eleccioun for in suche reulynge cyteseyns chesen hem a lord.
Herby the dyuersite is iknowe betweyne rewlyng paternale by the
whiche the fader rewleth the child and the rewlyng nupciale by the
whiche the housebonde rewleth the wif, for the fader hath more maystrie
and more hool and ful rewlyng ot the child thanne the housebonde ot the
wif. Also the fadres lordschipe of the child is more kynde lordschipe
thanne the housebondes lordschipe ouer the wif, for in som wise the wif
is acounted pere to the housebonde and cheseth here an housebonde.
And children ben not icounted peres to the fader nother cheseth hem a
fader but thei ben kyndeliche igendred and cometh ot the fader. thanne
the lordschipe paternale that the fader hath ot oon child is more kynde
lich than the lordschip coniugale that the housebond hath ot the wif.
For theis a man be kyndelich desposed to wedloc, sif that he hath this
womman or thulke to wyf is at his owne wille and free eleccioun. [So
as a man is kyndelich ydowede to spekyng, theigh he speke this proper
langage other that, it is at his owne wille and free eleccioun.] thanne the
rewelyng coniugale is not so kyndelich as the rewlyng paternale, for in
no wise children chesen hem a fader.
It is iknowe how rewelyng coniugale and the rewelyng paternale ben
diuerse by the manere ot rewlyng, for the oon is more symple and
kyndelich and the other is more parciale and by eleccioun; it may be
sone iknowe how this twey manere ot rewlyng ben diuerse by workes
and dedes. For the fader scholde so rewle the children that he scholde
ordeyne hem to othere workes and dedes than his wif, for children
scholde lerne workys and dedes ot cheualrye] and ot cyuel and dure
suche workes and dedes whan they ben of age and wyues scholde not
lerne suche workes and dedes for he schulde not vse suche workes
and dedes.
thanne it is iknowe that al citeseins scholde reule here wifes and chil
dren by dyuerse manere rewlyng but that is most semelich for kynges
and princes for thei scholde keepe and holde kynde resoun

Chapter XV
It was iseid tofore that in an hous ben diuerse maneres ot rewlyng:
the rewlyng nupciale by the whiche the housebonde rewleth the wif,
the rewlyng paternal by the whiche the fader rewleth the child, and the
rewlyng domynatiuum that is lordes rewle by the whiche a lord rewleth
his seruantes. Panne after, we hauen distyngwed bytwene rewlynges
coniugale, that is rewlyng ot wedloc, and paternale, that is fader rewlyng,
[for paternale] is more ful and hool rewlyng and symple withoute
condicioun, and the rewlyng nupciale is parciale. And for the paternale
rewlyng is more kyndelich and the nupciale rewlyng is in som wise by
eleccioun, also for wif and seruant ben iordeyned to dyuerse workes
and dedes, it is to declarynge how the wif and seruant scholde be
diuersliche irewled. And that a man scholde not bylede his wif as a
seruant we may preue by thre weyes: the firste is itake by kynde ordre,
the seconde by perfeccioun ot hous, the thridde by that the housebonde
and wif ben peres
the firste mene is declared in this wise. For al the hool kynde is imeued
and irewled by God and by angelis; and as the philosofre seith in libro
De Fortuna, the kynde inclynacioun and excityng that we hauen in the
soule we hauen of God as of hym that meueth] al the hole kynde. thanne
